entry.evidence: to elucidate the mechanism of tectonic tremors, which typically involve the presence of water

sequences.source_document: Iwamoto et al. 2022, Sci. Rep. 12:6234 (publisher XML text)

steps.action: Took the tremor epicentre catalogue of Wech (2016), which places tremors only above the subducted Yakutat terrane, and noted that few volcanoes lie above it.
steps.quote: Tectonic tremors occur only on the side of the subducted Yakutat terrane.

steps.action: Took the prior 3-D thermal and dehydration model of Qu et al. (2021) for the region to the southwest, which puts full slab dehydration at 60-100 km depth.
steps.quote: They concluded that the slab was fully dehydrated at slab surface depths ranging from 60 to 100 km

steps.action: Built on the authors' own earlier 3-D thermomechanical model of simultaneous Yakutat and Pacific subduction and its interplate temperature estimates.
steps.quote: Iwamoto et al.8 constructed a 3-D thermomechanical model that was [...] with the simultaneous subduction of the Yakutat terrane and Pacific plate

steps.action: Posed the question of how slab dehydration relates to the tremor distribution and the volcanic chain, adding a marine sedimentary layer and plate-specific layer thicknesses.
steps.quote: We discuss the relationships among dehydration and tectonic tremors and volcanic chains in the Alaska subduction zone.

steps.action: Ran four finite-difference thermomechanical models with effective friction coefficients 0.0085-0.02125 (pore fluid pressure ratio 0.975-0.990) and selected mu' = 0.01275 by the smallest weighted RMS misfit to observed heat flow (Methods §5.1 ¶3, §5.2 ¶1; Table S2).
steps.quote: selected the most suitable model with the smallest weighted root mean square (RMS) value of the residuals between the observed and calculated heat flows

steps.action: Compared the new model with the earlier model, which differs only in the Yakutat slab geometry: slab temperatures are up to 100-200 °C lower where the geometry changed, but the interplate event temperatures are unchanged (Figs. S1, S2).
steps.quote: the temperature ranges of the interplate seismic events are exactly the same as those obtained from Iwamoto et al.8

steps.action: Described the present-day slab temperature field at 0, 6 and 10 km below the slab surface: temperatures rise with depth and are lower in the older Yakutat terrane.
steps.quote: the surface temperatures of the subducted Yakutat terrane tend to be lower than those of the Pacific plate for the same depth

steps.action: Set the auxiliary assumption that the Alaskan tremors, whose depths are undetermined, lie at the plate interface, as Ide (2012) found in other subduction zones.
steps.quote: we assumed that the tectonic tremors in south-central Alaska take place at the plate interface

steps.action: Read the modelled slab-surface temperature at each tremor epicentre and obtained a tremor temperature range.
steps.quote: the temperature range at the locations of the tectonic tremors was estimated to be 484 ± 71 (1σ) °C

steps.action: Adopted the published mechanism that slab dehydration water lowers effective normal stress and causes tremors (Obara 2002), and hypothesised that the thicker Yakutat sediment and crust change the water distribution.
steps.quote: We considered that the differences in the thicknesses of these layers would affect the water content distributions in the Yakutat terrane and Pacific plate.

steps.action: Computed water content from the model p-T field in a three-layer slab (sediment 2/6 km, crust 5/25 km for Pacific/Yakutat), using turbidite, MORB and ultramafic phase diagrams.
steps.quote: [...] the slab into three layers, namely, the marine sedimentary layer, oceanic crust, and slab mantle

steps.action: Compared the water-content maps and sections with the tremor area: water content changes near the downdip side of the tremor zone, from turbidite and MORB phase transformations (Figure 3, p. 5).
steps.quote: At a depth of 6 km from the slab surface, the water contents change significantly near the downdip side of the tectonic tremor-generating area

steps.action: Computed the dehydration gradient, the change in water content per unit length along the subduction direction, for each layer.
steps.quote: we calculated the differences in water content per unit length in the subduction direction, which are referred to as the dehydration gradient13

steps.action: Compared the dehydration-gradient maps and sections with the tremor area: sediment dehydration spans the zone, crustal dehydration peaks downdip, and three mantle bands appear (Figure 4, p. 6).
steps.quote: the dehydration gradients increase near the downdip side of the tectonic tremor-generating area

steps.action: Summed the dehydration gradients vertically from the slab surface to the slab Moho (7 km Pacific, 31 km Yakutat).
steps.quote: we calculated the vertical sum of the dehydration gradients from the slab surface to the slab Moho

steps.action: Found that the summed dehydration gradient is largest downdip of the tremor area, mainly from the 25-km Yakutat crust (Figure 5, p. 7).
steps.quote: the vertical sum of the dehydration gradients on the downdip side of the tectonic tremor area was the largest and was remarkable

steps.action: Recomputed the summed dehydration gradient with the Yakutat sediment thinned to 2 km; the pattern near the tremor zone did not change significantly (Fig. S4).
steps.quote: there were no significant differences from the distribution of the summed dehydration gradients shown in Fig. 5

steps.action: Compared results with Suenaga et al. (Kyushu tremor temperatures and phase change; Hikurangi gradient of the same order) and with Qu et al. (complete dehydration slightly deeper here, attributed to the turbidite layer and older Yakutat slab).
steps.quote: The depth at which dehydration was complete was slightly deeper than that reported by Qu et al.7.

steps.action: Kept the claim that dehydration water from the sediment and crust causes the tremors, and that tremors are confined to the Yakutat terrane because its thick, water-rich layers release more water.
steps.quote: the water that is produced by dehydration from the slab is considered to be responsible for the occurrence of the tectonic tremors

steps.action: Compared the Yakutat-Pacific contrast with the analogous Shikoku-Kyushu contrast in SW Japan, explained there by dehydration depth (Tatsumi et al. 2020).
steps.quote: In southwestern Japan, there are similar spatial changes in the features along the Nankai Trough12.

steps.action: Concluded that few volcanoes lie above the Yakutat terrane because little water remains beneath the arc, and suggested that Pacific slab-mantle dehydration at 80-100 km feeds the arc.
steps.quote: there are few volcanoes because little water remains in the subducted Yakutat terrane beneath them, where magma should be produced

tree.answer: Tremors confined to the subducted Yakutat terrane; few volcanoes above it
No; slab temperature and water content are inferred through a thermal model and phase diagrams
Explain the tremor and volcano distribution by slab dehydration
No rival mechanism stated; only the dehydration-water hypothesis is assessed
Not posed; no rival predictions computed
Conditions found: a natural subduction zone with two slab types side by side

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Analogous cases elsewhere (Kyushu, Hikurangi, SW Japan) are cited as consistent
Summed dehydration pattern unchanged when Yakutat sediment is thinned to 2 km; interplate temperatures unchanged by the new slab geometry
Dehydration explanation kept as the best account

end.claim: Dehydration of the thick Yakutat marine sedimentary layer and oceanic crust near the downdip edge of the tremor zone causes the tremors, which explains why tremors occur only above the Yakutat terrane; little water is left beneath the arc there, hence few volcanoes.

decisive_move.sentence: Computing water content and dehydration gradients from the calibrated thermal model in a three-layer slab with plate-specific sediment and crust thicknesses produced the spatial match with the tremor zone on which the claim rests.

gates.evidence: No data were acquired: the tremor catalogue (Wech) and heat flow are taken from others, and the hypothesis directed only the model set-up (layer thicknesses, §2.2 ¶1). The claim faced a spatial comparison it could in principle have failed (dehydration might not have coincided with the tremor zone) and one sensitivity test (§2.3 ¶3), but no match criterion or rival prediction was stated. Nothing is reported as fixed before the results; the friction coefficient was chosen after the heat-flow fit.

imports.item: finite-difference solution of the mass, momentum and energy equations as a time-marching problem
distance-weighted RMS misfit for model selection against heat flow

novelty_claims.quote: we newly introduced the marine sedimentary layer and included the thicknesses of the marine sedimentary layer and oceanic crust separately
we newly introduced the marine sedimentary layer in the top of the slab and used the turbidite phase diagram

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: (a) the tremor temperature 484 ± 71 °C is estimate_with_resolution, but the 1σ is the spread over tremor locations, not a model uncertainty, and it rests on the assumed plate-interface depth (§2.1 ¶3); (b) the arc-magma claim for the Pacific slab mantle is 'suggested' (§3 ¶7), weaker than best_explanation; (c) the interplate event temperatures are inherited from the authors' own earlier model (Iwamoto et al., under review). No rival mechanism for tremor confinement is stated or excluded (for example dip angle or temperature alone, though dip angle is mentioned in §3 ¶5), so composition is none_fits: a single forward-model consistency argument, with neither a crucial test nor repeated independent traces. The heat-flow comparison (§5.2 ¶1) is called an evaluation of validity, but it is the same data used to select mu'; I coded it as calibration (I), not as a V control (inference). The model's uncertainty in water content and the phase-diagram choices are not propagated. The match between dehydration and the tremor zone is judged visually from maps, with no quantitative criterion. The acknowledgements mention two referees, but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded and the changes made in review are unknown.

disagreements.target: Qu et al. 2021 (Appl. Sci.), complete slab dehydration at 60-100 km depth
disagreements.support: The authors' model puts complete dehydration at about 70-110 km, which they attribute to the added turbidite layer and phase diagram and to the older, colder Yakutat slab.
disagreements.quote: The depth at which dehydration was complete was slightly deeper than that reported by Qu et al.7.

disagreements.target: Iwamoto et al. (Tectonophysics, under review), the authors' earlier 3-D thermal model with a different Yakutat slab geometry
disagreements.support: With the slab interface up to about 30 km shallower in the northeast, the modelled slab-surface temperatures there are up to 100-200 °C lower, while the interplate event temperatures are unchanged.
disagreements.quote: the temperature distribution of the slab surface in our model is as great as 100–200 °C lower
